strengths: The paper targets an important problem: ML-based primal heuristics for MILP often ignore feasibility and non-binary integer variables, and the proposed RL formulation is a reasonable direction.

The two-phase reward design (feasibility first, then objective improvement) is an intuitive way to train an RL agent for MILP, and the use of a Transformer encoder over a bipartite graph is technically plausible for capturing long-range variable interactions.

The ablation study attempts to validate the key architectural components (periodic embedding, phase token, separated layers), and the results show all three are useful on the generated D100x50 dataset.
The method is able to find feasible solutions on all tested instances in the reported experiments, and it improves over MLP/CNN variants on the larger dataset.
The paper is generally well motivated and discusses why existing supervised prediction-based partial-solution approaches can struggle with feasibility and integer variables.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is not convincing for ICML: there is no comparison to existing ML/RL approaches for MILP (e.g., Gasse et al. 2019; Nair et al. 2020; Han et al. 2023; Qi et al. 2021; Smart Feasibility Pump), so the claimed novelty and superiority are unsupported.

The experiments use only small random instances (9x18 and 100x50) and no standard MILP benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB, ML4CO, combinatorial auctions). The data generation also constructs b = Aξ + ε with ξ integer, which guarantees a hidden feasible integer solution; this may make feasibility finding artificially easy.

Despite the title and abstract claiming mixed-integer linear programming, the method only considers the special case where all variables are non-binary integers. Continuous variables and mixed-integer problems are not addressed, limiting the scope of the contribution.

Reproducibility is insufficient: crucial training details are missing, including network dimensions, number of Transformer heads/layers, learning rate, batch size, number of training instances/episodes, hardware, and random seeds. No code or model release is mentioned.

The solution search strategy depends on an LP relaxation to obtain the initial solution and lower bound, meaning the method is not fully independent of traditional optimization solvers, contrary to the framing of end-to-end ML-based MILP solving.

The local search algorithm has an unspecified local region parameter Δ and a reset condition that may overly constrain exploration. No sensitivity analysis is provided for Δ, the action step size (fixed at 1), or the step limit.

The RP_Gap metric is defined relative to the best objective across compared methods rather than the true optimal solution; for D100x50, Gurobi has a nonzero gap of 0.01, yet the setup and time limits are not clearly described, making the reported comparisons hard to interpret.

Scalability is not demonstrated: the action space is 3^n and only n=100 is tested. There is no evidence the approach works on larger or structurally harder MILPs, and no training/inference time is reported.

The presentation has technical ambiguities: equations 7-8 are unclearly specified, the reward scaling in phase 1 is under-explained, and it is unclear how per-variable actions are jointly sampled and trained within the Actor-Critic framework.

There is no statistical analysis (e.g., confidence intervals, multiple seeds), and the test set size (100 random instances) is small. The conclusion acknowledges local search limitations but does not adequately discuss broader negative results or failure cases.

strengths: Targets an important limitation of existing ML-based primal heuristics: handling non-binary integer variables and producing complete feasible solutions rather than partial assignments.

The two-phase reward design (before/after first feasible solution) is a sensible way to balance feasibility search and objective improvement, and the RL formulation avoids the need for labeled optimal solutions.

The hybrid MPNN + Transformer encoder is a reasonable architectural choice for capturing both local constraint-variable interactions and global variable relationships; the ablation attempts to justify its components.
The proposed method achieves 100/100 feasible solutions on both tested synthetic datasets and finds optimal solutions on the small D9*18 dataset, showing the approach is not vacuous.
The paper honestly acknowledges key limitations, including the restriction to all-integer MILPs and the local-search nature of the method.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is far too narrow to support the paper's broad claims. It uses only two synthetic, randomly generated datasets (D9*18 and D100*50) and no standard MILP benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB, NeurIPS ML4CO) or real-world instances. Real MILPs are much larger and more diverse, so scalability and generalization remain unproven.

Missing comparisons to prior ML-based primal heuristics and RL-for-MILP methods (e.g., Gasse et al. 2019, Nair et al. 2020, Han et al. 2023, Yoon 2022, Qi et al. 2021). The only learned baselines are architectural variants of the proposed method (M_MLP, M_CNN), so the paper does not establish an advantage over existing learning approaches; there is also no classical local-search or rounding/feasibility-pump baseline to isolate the contribution of RL.

The claim of solving MILP 'end-to-end based solely on ML' and 'without delegating sub-problems to traditional solvers' is misleading. The algorithm obtains the initial solution and lower bound obj_r from the LP relaxation, which normally requires a traditional LP solver (likely Gurobi). LP relaxation is a traditional optimization subroutine, and the paper does not report or account for its runtime, so the end-to-end claim is unsupported.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper omits code, network sizes/layer dimensions, hyperparameters, random seeds, training compute, stopping thresholds, LP solver details, and full runtime comparisons. The reported training is measured in 'parameter updates' (500/5,000) rather than standard epochs/steps, making the setup hard to reproduce or compare.

The evidence that the RL agent learns meaningful relationships between variables and constraints is weak. The local-search procedure (Algorithm 1) uses handcrafted local-region size Delta and hard resets when outside the target objective interval; the reward function in phase2 depends on the LP lower bound and current best. The ablations only test architectural components, not whether RL is necessary versus a simple local search or heuristic control policy.

The reported gains are small and lack statistical support. On D100*50, the proposed method reaches 1.33% RP_Gap versus 1.60% for M_MLP, while Gurobi achieves 0.01%; no error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are provided. Since all learning methods already achieve 100% FR and sub-second FFST, the practical advantage is unclear.

The action space and search strategy limit scalability: each variable can only increase/decrease by 1 or stay unchanged, and the Transformer encoder attends over variable nodes with O(n^2) complexity. This is unlikely to scale to large integer ranges or large MILPs, yet no experiments probe larger n, denser constraints, or continuous variables.

There are presentation and notation issues that impede verification: e.g., the reformulation example incorrectly writes 'minimizing -2x3 -3x2 + x3' instead of -2x1 -3x2 + x3; the notation for f_t and its scaled version is inconsistent; the condition in Algorithm 1 line 13 is ambiguous; and Table 3/Table 2 formatting reduces clarity. These issues, while fixable, further undermine confidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: ML-based primal heuristics for MILP and the difficulty of maintaining feasibility for non-binary integer variables.

It proposes a complete RL-based solution-search framework rather than a partial-solution prediction followed by a traditional MILP solve, and formulates two-phase rewards to distinguish feasibility discovery from objective improvement.

The GNN architecture combines a bipartite message-passing GCN with a Transformer encoder, and uses periodic embeddings for scalar features; the architectural ablation is a reasonable attempt to justify design choices.
The experimental results report 100/100 feasible rate and competitive RP_Gap compared with MLP/CNN variants on the generated datasets, with optimal solutions on the small D_9x18 setting.
The paper honestly discusses some limitations, such as the restricted local-search neighborhood and the restriction to integer variables with future extension to continuous variables.
weaknesses: The central claim of solving MILP end-to-end without delegating to traditional solvers is not supported: Algorithm 1 line 1 obtains both the initial solution and the lower bound from LP relaxation, which is itself a traditional optimization routine. The method also only handles pure integer problems, not general MILP with continuous variables, despite the title and abstract.

The generated benchmark instances are too weak to support the feasibility claims. With A entries positive, b=Aξ+ε with positive ξ, ε, and x≥0, the all-zero solution always satisfies Ax≤b, so feasibility is trivial. No equality constraints, negative coefficients, standard MIPLIB instances, or real-world problems are used.

There is no comparison to state-of-the-art ML-based MILP solvers or primal heuristics (e.g., Gasse et al. 2019; Nair et al. 2020; Han et al. 2023; Cantürk et al. 2024) or to RL-based feasibility-pump methods (Qi et al. 2021), despite directly positioning itself against them. The only strong baseline, Gurobi, achieves much better RP_Gap on D_100x50 (0.01 vs. 1.33).

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no seeds, no error bars, no significance tests, and RP_Gap is measured relative to the best method rather than a known optimum, making the reported near-optimality difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Important hyperparameters, network sizes, attention-head counts, learning rates, local-region size Δ, time/step limits, and termination conditions are omitted, and no code or data release is indicated.

The RL formulation is under-specified. The action space is joint over n variables (3^n possibilities), but it is unclear how the Actor factorizes actions, how the Critic estimates Q(S,A) over joint actions, and how credit assignment is performed over variables.

The phase2 reward has technical issues: δ_b is claimed to lie in [0,1], but |obj_t−obj_b|/|obj_b| can exceed 1; boundary cases such as obj_t below obj_r or above obj_b are not fully handled; and the +1 improvement bonus is not analyzed for scale relative to penalties.

Presentation quality is weakened by citation-year errors and typos, e.g., “Bertsimas [2024]” for a 1997 reference, “Nair et al. (1997)” for 2020, “Vaswani (1975)” for 2017, “Han et al. [2015]” for 2023, and an objective reformulation typo using −2x3 instead of −2x1.

The ablation results are surprising and insufficiently explained: removing phase token or separated layers yields 0/100 feasible rate, which conflicts with the trivial feasibility of x=0 on these instances and suggests fragile training rather than a clear architectural necessity.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: developing a full end-to-end reinforcement learning solver for mixed-integer/linear integer programs without delegating the remaining MILP subproblem to an off-the-shelf solver.

Proposes a coherent RL formulation with a two-phase reward design that separates finding the first feasible solution from improving solution quality, and an action space based on incrementing/decrementing/no-changing integer variables.

Combines local MPNN message passing with a Transformer encoder to capture both local constraint-variable relations and longer-range variable interactions; ablation studies attempt to justify each component.

Reports 100% feasible rates on all generated datasets and near-optimal gaps on small instances, with faster first feasible solution times than a 100-second/600-second Gurobi baseline in the reported tables.

Provides useful background on MILP bipartite graph representation and includes a proof that any improving feasible solution must lie between the LP-relaxation bound and the current best objective value, which motivates the reward shaping.
weaknesses: The central claim of solving MILP without relying on off-the-shelf solvers is questionable: Algorithm 1 uses a Relaxation(M) step to obtain the initial solution x0 and LP-relaxation objective obj_r, which is typically computed by a traditional LP solver such as Gurobi. The paper never specifies how this LP relaxation is obtained, nor does it exclude solver time from the reported FFST. If Gurobi or another LP solver is used for relaxation, the method is not fully end-to-end and the main contribution is overstated.

The evaluation is restricted to synthetic, randomly generated all-integer instances created by the authors. It does not test on standard MILP benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB) or real-world MILP formulations, despite motivating the work with logistics, maritime transportation, and energy systems. The method is also not evaluated on genuinely mixed-integer problems with continuous variables, so the title and claims about MILP are broader than the actual evidence.

The comparison baselines are weak for a paper claiming a new state-of-the-art direction: M_MLP and M_CNN are architecture ablations rather than established learning-based MILP solvers, and LS is a simple local search. The paper does not compare against relevant partial end-to-end or ML-based primal heuristics such as Gasse et al. (2019), Nair et al. (2020), Han et al. (2023), Cantürk et al. (2024), or the RL feasibility pump of Qi et al. (2021), even though these are directly related.

The practical significance is not convincingly demonstrated: Gurobi solves all generated datasets to near-zero gap in under one second according to Table 1, while the proposed method has larger gaps (up to 0.55%) and likely uses 100 seconds or more for optimization. The advantage is mainly faster first feasible solution time, not better final solution quality, and the tested instances are small enough that commercial solvers are already effectively instantaneous.

The claim of '(near-)optimal' solutions is not rigorously supported. For larger datasets, the gap is computed relative to a best-known solution that includes Gurobi's 600-second result, not a verified optimum, and there are no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or per-instance distributions. Proposition 1 is mathematically trivial and does not provide optimality guarantees for the learned solver.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The manuscript does not release code or provide complete architecture and training details (e.g., exact Transformer/MPNN hyperparameters, training time, number of training instances, LP relaxation implementation, handling of infinite bounds and equality constraints). Hyperparameters are partially described, but the LP solver used for relaxation and the exact evaluation protocol remain unclear.

Presentation and internal consistency issues reduce confidence: some reward equations (Eqs. 12-13) are garbled or hard to parse; the text mentions beta values {0.3, 0.6} while Table 1 reports 0.5; Table 1 lacks the #win metric despite it being introduced; and assumptions such as all-integer variables, unbounded upper bounds, and generated constraint structure are not fully discussed as limitations.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations section and does not discuss failure modes, scaling to larger problems, training cost, or negative societal/environmental implications of learned MILP solvers. The claimed first-ness and broad applicability are not appropriately qualified.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine gap in the literature: existing ML-based primal heuristics for MILP mostly produce partial solutions, focus on binary variables, and delegate the rest to a solver; the authors propose a full end-to-end RL search over all variables including general integer ones, which is a worthwhile direction.

The technical pipeline is competently assembled: bipartite graph representation of MILP, a hybrid MPNN + Transformer encoder, Periodic Embeddings for unbounded scalar features, and a phase-aware actor/critic design. Section 3.2 gives a coherent account of how these pieces fit together (Fig. 5).

The experimental section is relatively complete in scope, covering four synthetic dataset sizes (D9x18 up to D300x100), multiple values of the toward-optimal bias beta, an ablation over architectural components (TE, MP, PE, SL, PT in Table 3), and a neighborhood-size study (Table 2).
The authors explicitly acknowledge that guaranteeing optimality for neural CO solvers remains open (Section 4.3), which is an honest treatment of limitations.
weaknesses: The central claim that the RL-MILP solver 'achieves (near-)optimal solutions' is not meaningful as evidence of a contribution because Gurobi solves every instance in <1s with essentially 0% Gap (Table 1). On D9x18 all methods, including Gurobi, score ~0.00-0.15%; on larger sets Gurobi scores 0.01-0.03% while the RL solver scores 0.34-0.55%. The RL solver therefore offers no demonstrated advantage on any dimension (feasibility, time, or quality) over a trivial commercial LP/MILP solve. ML-based heuristics are motivated by instances where traditional solvers are slow or fail; no such instance is presented, so the main motivation is untested.

The Gap metric is defined relative to a BKS that is 'the best value obtained among all compared methods, including Gurobi with a 600-second time limit,' which includes the RL solver's own best solutions. This confounds the comparison (a method can inflate BKS and shrink its own Gap). No seeds, standard deviations, or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, so differences such as 0.00% vs 0.01-0.02% between Ours and M_MLP are within any plausible noise.

Feasibility is not actually hard on the evaluated distribution. All instances use l_i = 0, u_i = infinity, c in [-10, 1], A > 0 with b = Lambda*xi + eps (Appendix E.1), which makes the feasible region very permissive; this contradicts the paper's central pitch that feasibility for integer variables is critical. Results on this narrow synthetic distribution say little about the claimed real-world logistics/maritime/energy cases, and generalization to other distributions or sizes is never tested.

The 'theoretical foundation' of Proposition 1 is essentially the textbook LP-relaxation bound (obj_r <= obj' < obj_b). It provides no guarantee about feasibility or optimality of the learned agent and does not constitute the kind of theory the contribution list implies. The reward derivations in Eq. 6-15 rely on this trivial bound and on arbitrary constants (e.g., the -10 no-change penalty) that are not justified.

The novelty over the closest prior work (Qi et al. 2021, Smart Feasibility Pump) is incremental. The manuscript itself states that prior RL work 'focuses solely on finding the first feasible solution,' so the delta is essentially adding a phase2 optimization reward. Given that Qi et al. already demonstrated RL for MILP feasibility, the incremental extension is modest and would need much stronger evidence to be publishable at ICML.

The claim of 'without reliance on off-the-shelf solvers' is overstated. The method consumes obj_r from an LP relaxation (Algorithm 1, line 3) and builds its reward (Eq. 12-14) directly on this bound; the LP relaxation is obtained from a solver. This is a material dependence that the abstract/pitch suppress.

Scalability is not addressed. The method takes an action for each of the n variables at every step and searches by local +/-Delta moves in integer space; the largest tested instance is 300x100. No analysis or experiment addresses how this scales to the thousands of variables typical of real MILP applications, and training cost (5,000-10,000 parameter updates on 64 concurrent instances) is never budgeted against Gurobi's solve time.

Baseline comparisons are weak. LS is given a feasible start from the RL agent and its naive single-variable neighborhood, so outperforming it is not informative. M_CNN collapses to 0-4% FR at larger sizes and is retained in the tables as a straw man, while the only truly competitive comparator (Gurobi) is not evaluated on hard regimes.

Presentation problems compound the above: inconsistent use of beta values across text and tables (0.3/0.5/0.6/0.8), undefined symbol usage in the reward section, and unsupported summary claims in the abstract ('up to 100x' style figures are used without a corresponding experiment). These make it hard for readers to reproduce or verify the reported numbers.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: learning to solve MILP/ILP without delegating the remaining MILP to a traditional solver, using a phase-based RL formulation and dedicated reward design.

Proposes a Transformer+GNN architecture to capture long-range variable-constraint interactions, with an ablation over architecture components such as Transformer encoder, MPNN, periodic embedding, separated actor/critic layers, and phase token.
Experimental results on synthetic random instances show 100% feasibility rate, sub-second first feasible solution time, and relative gaps below 1% for larger instances.
Provides a detailed RL system design including action space, reward functions, search strategy, and pseudo-code for learning and solution search.
Analyzes the effect of the toward-optimal bias parameter and neighborhood size, showing that larger action sets can improve solution quality.
Reproducibility is partly supported by documenting instance generation, hyperparameters, and implementation components.
weaknesses: Critical integrality handling is not described: the algorithm starts from an LP relaxation solution x0 and updates variables only by integer increments (+/-1, etc.), but if x0 is fractional, the fractional part is preserved, so the method cannot reach an integer-feasible solution without an unstated rounding or integrality-projection step.

The synthetic dataset is trivially feasible because the constraint matrix entries and right-hand sides are positive, making x=0 always feasible. Thus the reported 100% feasible rate and short FFST do not demonstrate hard feasibility discovery, which is a central motivation of the paper.

The paper claims to solve MILP, but all variables are integers, making the experiments an ILP special case. No continuous variables are included, so the method is not evaluated on genuinely mixed-integer problems.

Despite claiming to operate 'without relying on off-the-shelf solvers,' the method uses an LP relaxation solution and obj_r, which typically requires a traditional LP/MILP solver. This delegation is not clearly acknowledged or discussed.

Evaluation is limited to small/medium synthetic datasets generated from the same distribution; there are no standard MILP benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB), real-world instances, or cross-size/cross-distribution generalization tests.

Baselines are weak: M_MLP and M_CNN are internal architecture variants, and LS is warm-started from the proposed agent's feasible solution. No comparison against strong learning-based primal heuristics or recent neural MILP solvers is provided.
The theoretical foundation is weak: Proposition 1 is essentially the standard LP-relaxation lower-bound property and does not guarantee feasibility, convergence, or optimality of the RL search.

Results do not report variance across seeds, training time, time-to-best-solution, or statistical significance; reproducibility is incomplete without code release or full architectural/training details.

The comparison with Gurobi is unfavorable: Gurobi solves all instances in under one second with 0.00-0.03% gap, while the proposed method has larger gaps (up to ~0.55%) on larger datasets, so the practical advantage is unclear.

Presentation has inconsistencies and unclear claims, e.g., the ablation discussion of removing the Transformer encoder versus the MPNN is not aligned with the table values, and the title/framing overstates MILP generality.

strengths: Proposes a novel RL-based start primal heuristic that can generate feasible ILP solutions independently, including for non-binary integer variables, which is an underexplored and important setting.

The two-phase reward design and constraint-aware variable/neighbor selection are sensible and tailored to ILP feasibility search; the Transformer-based GNN is motivated by long-range variable interactions and supported by ablation.
Empirical results on five benchmark families show 100% feasibility rate and competitive primal gap/primal integral against SCIP start heuristics and PAS+SCIP, especially for non-binary integers.
The paper provides implementation details, hyperparameters, and training times, and uses open-source solver/tool components, making a reproduction attempt plausible.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated: RL for feasibility pump / learning feasibility for (mixed) integer programming was already explored by Qi et al. (2021) ('Smart Feasibility Pump'), which is cited only incidentally for NBI generation and not compared. The claim of being the first E2EPH method to explicitly learn feasibility is therefore questionable.

The theoretical guarantee (Proposition 1) is weak and conditional: it assumes R_const > 0 and R_bound = 0 for all t < T, i.e., it assumes the agent takes actions that strictly improve feasibility. It does not guarantee that the learned policy will produce such actions, nor does it address finite-time convergence under the actual stochastic policy.

Evaluation is potentially unfair regarding time and excluded failures: PG and PI are averaged only over instances where at least one feasible solution is found, so methods with low feasibility rates can appear competitive on the subset they solve while failing elsewhere. RL-SPH also stops only after all baselines finish, which may give it a different time budget than individual baselines.

Primal integral definition and computation are underspecified and non-standard: PI(T) = sum PG(obj_t) with PG=1 if no feasible solution is available, but it is unclear whether timesteps are seconds, iterations, or solver nodes, and the values are not time-normalized. This makes PI comparisons across methods with different runtimes difficult to interpret.

The reward function contains many hand-tuned components and inconsistencies: the phase-1 conditions appear to use 'forall i' where Algorithm 1 uses existential bound violation, and the -100 no-change penalty and alpha=2 bias are not deeply justified. Sensitivity analysis is limited to alpha only.

The experimental evaluation is limited to randomly generated benchmark instances and synthetic NBI instances. There is no evaluation on standard hard MILP benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB) or real-world instances, limiting evidence that the method generalizes beyond the generated distributions.

The combined RL-SPH+SCIP experiment fixes variables based on RL-SPH solutions generated in the first five seconds, but the comparison against PAS+S and SCIP is not fully controlled. It is unclear whether PAS+S receives a comparable warm start or how much the reported improvement depends on the additional RL-SPH preprocessing time.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code link or model checkpoints are provided for RL-SPH, and key training details such as random seeds, policy sampling, and exact variable-selection sampling procedure are not fully specified. The RL agent may be sensitive to stochastic training.

Presentation issues affect clarity: inconsistent notation (e.g., 'l_i l u_i'), asymmetric error bars such as '0.14+0.59-0.14', and confusing descriptions of bound-violation conditions make parts of the method and results harder to verify.

The headline claims ('44x lower primal gap', '2.3x lower primal integral') are not clearly supported by the reported tables and appear to depend on which baseline subset is chosen; the abstract/conclusion overstate the empirical evidence.

strengths: Targets a genuinely under-explored setting: end-to-end primal heuristics for ILP with non-binary integer variables, which most prior E2EPH work (and PAS) cannot handle.
RL-SPH achieves 100% feasibility rate across the reported benchmarks without delegating feasibility to an external solver, which is a meaningful capability if it holds up.
The combination with a solver (RL-SPH+S) yields clear gains in primal integral on IS and NBI, and the Transformer-based encoder is shown to matter in the ablation (models without it fail on CA).
The paper is organized and the two-phase reward and search strategy are described in reasonable detail, with pseudocode and appendices.
weaknesses: Proposition 1 is essentially circular and does not establish the claimed feasibility guarantee. The premise already assumes constraint/bound reward improvement ('R_const > 0 and R_bound = 0 for all t < T'), from which convergence to feasibility follows trivially. The premise (monotone feasibility improvement at every step) is not something the trained agent is shown to satisfy, so the 'theoretically guaranteeing feasibility' claim is vacuous and overstated.

The baseline comparison is artificially set up in a way that favors RL-SPH: SCIP's native heuristics (Diving, FP, Rounding, RENS) are run with presolving and branching disabled, which cripples them relative to normal usage, while RL-SPH 'stops when all baseline methods complete their search,' giving it an unbounded time budget. This confounds the head-to-head claims.

Headline claims are misleading because they are averaged across benchmarks. The '44× lower primal gap' and '2.3× lower primal integral' figures mask that on SC, RL-SPH(LP) is far worse than FP (9.67 vs 0.34) and Diving (0.00), and its PI is worse than Diving/FP/RENS. Aggregate multipliers of this kind are not a faithful summary.

Limited novelty. RL for learning feasibility in MILP primal heuristics has been explored before (e.g., Smart Feasibility Pump, Qi et al. 2021), and the 'first E2EPH method that explicitly learns feasibility' claim is not adequately substantiated against this and related prior work.

Evaluation is thin and possibly unreliable: only 100 test instances per benchmark, BKS defined as the best value among the compared methods (a relative, method-dependent target rather than a true best-known solution, which makes PG easy to distort), and only a single E2EPH baseline (PAS).

The reward design (Eqs. 2–8) is a complex, ad-hoc construction with several hand-tuned constants (-100, α=2, √n̂ scaling) and little justification or sensitivity analysis beyond α in Appendix F; the phase-1 case analysis with overlapping conditions is hard to verify.

Reproducibility and presentation problems: unfamiliar and inconsistent error notation ('0.14+0.59-0.14', '3.82+9.77-3.82') that does not match the ± used elsewhere, inconsistent notation throughout (lhs/Ihs, 'l_i l u_i', garbled citations such as 'Shoja and Akehill', Berthold cited both as a thesis and a paper), and a stated benchmark count (four) that does not match the five benchmarks actually used.

Key mechanisms are underspecified: how RL-SPH+S fixes variables from an 'ensemble of feasible solutions' and what 'unanimous value' means is not defined precisely enough to reproduce, and no code/artifact release is indicated.

strengths: Addresses an important gap in learning-based primal heuristics: existing E2EPH methods usually cannot independently produce feasible solutions and mainly handle binary variables, while RL-SPH targets general integer ILPs.

Proposes a novel RL-based start primal heuristic that operates without labeled near-optimal solutions and combines phase-specific reward shaping, variable selection, and a Transformer-based GNN to capture long-range variable-constraint dependencies.

Reports strong empirical results in several settings: 100% feasibility rate on five benchmarks and improved primal gap / primal integral over common start primal heuristics on IS, CA, and MVC, with especially clear gains on MVC and IS.

The ablation study provides some evidence that the proposed GNN components (Transformer encoder, reward context, phase-separated layers) matter, and the method is motivated with relevant background on start primal heuristics and bipartite graph representations.
The paper is generally well motivated and addresses a practically relevant case: non-binary integer variables, which are important in logistics, energy, and maritime transportation applications.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not sound. Proposition 1 assumes R_{t,const} > 0 and R_{t,bound} = 0 for all t < T, then concludes that x_T is feasible. Even granting monotonic improvement and an upper bound of 0, the sequence sum_j min(f_{t,j},0) need not reach 0 at a finite T; the argument conflates limit behavior with finite-time feasibility. Therefore the stated guarantee that a well-trained agent will discover a feasible solution is unsupported.

The reward definitions are complex and contain ambiguous or likely inconsistent notation. For example, Eq. (7) uses the condition (x_i notin [l_i, u_i] for all i) to prioritize bound satisfaction, whereas the text appears to mean that any variable bound is violated. Such a condition materially changes the intended behavior and makes the reward design harder to reproduce and verify.

The primal integral metric is non-standard and potentially unfair. Defining PI(T)=sum_t PG(obj_t) without time normalization or a clear timestep discretization can make comparisons dependent on stopping criteria and solve-time distributions, especially when baselines run up to 1000 seconds and RL-SPH stops when the baselines finish.

The empirical comparison may overstate the headline numbers. The claimed 44x lower PG and 2.3x lower PI appear to be averaged only over methods with 100% feasibility, but on SC, FP achieves PG 0.34 with 99% FR while RL-SPH(LP) achieves PG 9.67; Diving achieves PG 0.00 with only 1% FR. The aggregate therefore depends heavily on which subset is compared, and no significance tests or confidence intervals are reported.

The solver-integration experiment is limited. RL-SPH+S is evaluated on only IS and NBI; for NBI there is no PAS+S baseline because PAS does not support non-binary integers, so the solver comparison reduces to RL-SPH+S vs SCIP with only modest PG difference (0.23 vs 0.24). The variable-fixing procedure using the first five seconds of RL-SPH(LP) solutions is not described in enough detail to assess fairness or generality.

The ablation study is incomplete. It is conducted only on IS and CA, defines BKS among the compared models within 50 seconds rather than true best-known solutions, and does not isolate the effects of periodic embedding, scaling choices, variable-selection parameters, or the reward design across all benchmarks.

Related work and originality claims need more care. Prior RL for MIP feasibility pump (e.g., Qi et al., 2021) and other RL-based primal heuristics are not discussed in sufficient depth, and the claim of being the first E2EPH method to explicitly learn feasibility may be overstated unless distinguished clearly from those lines of work.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The paper mentions implementation libraries and some hyperparameters, but no code release, random seeds for ML training, exact reward thresholds, or inference-time measurements are provided. Combined with the notation issues, this makes it difficult for others to build reliably on the method.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: independently generating feasible ILP solutions, including non-binary integer variables, without relying on external solvers.
Provides extensive empirical evaluation across five CO benchmarks, multiple SPH baselines, three E2EPH methods, cross-problem/MIPLIB tests, robustness studies, solver integration, and ablations.

Reports 100% feasibility rate on all five benchmarks and often strong primal gap/primal integral improvements over strong start primal heuristics such as RHF, with fast first-feasible times in many settings.
The feasibility-aware variable selection and two-phase reward design are supported by ablations (Uniform vs F-aware, ILP-GT component analysis).
Handles non-binary integer domains, where many E2EPH methods are inapplicable, and demonstrates some generalization to MIPLIB instances, distribution shifts, and size/density changes.
Training does not require near-optimal labels and is computationally cheaper than some E2EPH baselines; hyperparameters are kept consistent across datasets.
The appendix provides useful reproducibility details, including datasets, hyperparameters, environment, training times, complexity analysis, and honest limitations.
weaknesses: Proposition 1 is assumption-laden and weak: it assumes R_t,const > 0 and R_t,bound = 0 for all t < T, which already encodes feasibility-directed behavior. The proof only shows cumulative violation decreases to zero under that assumption, not that the learned reward-maximizing policy will satisfy it. The claimed 'theoretical reward-feasibility alignment' is overstated.

The E2EPH comparison may be partially unfair: the SC and CA datasets differ substantially from those used in DiffILO/DDIM/PAS, and baselines use default configurations rather than dataset-specific tuning. DiffILO's 0% FR on SC/CA may reflect distribution shift and insufficient tuning, so the claim of outperforming SOTA E2EPH is not fully established for comparable settings.

The 100% FR is empirical only; there is no formal feasibility guarantee. Termination and time-limit protocols vary across experiments (e.g., RL-SPH stops when baselines finish; different time limits in Tables 1 and 2), and PG/PI are averaged only over feasible instances, which can flatter methods that find feasibility late.

Baseline construction is nonstandard: grouping 15 diving and 6 rounding SCIP heuristics into families and disabling presolving/branching may not reflect their true standalone performance, and it is unclear how resources are allocated among enabled heuristics.

There is no direct architecture-level comparison between ILP-GT and standard MPNN/GNN alternatives for ILP; the claim that a Graph Transformer is specifically necessary is supported mainly by internal component ablation.

Reproducibility of RL-SPH itself is limited: no artifact/code release link is mentioned, random seeds for RL training are not specified, and some reward constants and scaling choices appear arbitrary and may affect results.

Scalability remains limited: MIPLIB performance is mixed and often worse than RHF on large instances such as scpk4 and toll-like, while the main results do not demonstrate success at the 100k-variable scale; quadratic attention and O(mn) variable selection are acknowledged bottlenecks.

Some abstract/introduction claims (e.g., 28.6x lower primal gap and 2.6x lower primal integral) are not transparently traceable from the presented tables and are computed under heterogeneous baselines and stopping conditions.

The reward design introduces many hand-tuned constants and priorities; sensitivity analyses show performance can degrade with different alpha or neighbor ratios, so robustness across ILP families is not fully established.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: quickly generating feasible solutions for ILP and extending learning-based heuristics to non-binary integer variables.
Proposes RL-SPH, an actor-critic method with a graph-transformer policy and two-phase reward, and reports 100% feasibility rate on five benchmarks in the main tables.
Provides extensive empirical studies: cross-problem generalization, distribution/size/density shifts, MIPLIB tests, solver integration, hyperparameter analyses, and ablations (Tables 4-6, 13-20).
Training is relatively efficient (23-83 minutes per dataset, Table 9) and avoids supervised labels; the authors report speedups over PAS, DDIM, and DiffILO (Table 10).
Ablations suggest the feasibility-aware variable selection and transformer components contribute to performance (Tables 5 and 6).
The paper is transparent about several limitations (action magnitude, scalability, nonlinear constraints) and includes detailed appendices.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is essentially vacuous: Proposition 1 assumes R_const>0 and R_bound=0 for all t<T, i.e., it assumes the constraint violation strictly decreases at every step; the proof then shows violation eventually reaches zero. It does not show that reward maximization induces such a trajectory, so the claimed 'reward-feasibility alignment' is unsupported.

The feasibility benchmarks are misleadingly easy: for IS, SC, CA, and NBI, x=0 is feasible, and for MVC, x=1 is feasible; in NBI, b=Aξ+ε with ξ_i>=1 makes the all-ones vector feasible. Thus the 100% FR results do not demonstrate a solution to a hard feasibility problem; the real challenge is solution quality.

On the only non-binary benchmark (NBI), where the paper claims a key advantage, RHF achieves PG 0.00 while RL-SPH(LP) obtains PG 0.22 and RL-SPH(Random) 28.32 (Table 1); the RL method is not superior on this benchmark and the feasibility claim is not meaningful.

The comparison with E2EPH baselines is not convincing: PAS, DDIM, and DiffILO are evaluated on datasets with different sizes/characteristics from their original studies (e.g., SC 3,000 vs 2,000 variables; CA 4,000 vs 1,500 variables; Table 11), and the paper acknowledges DiffILO required dataset-specific tuning. Their failures on SC/CA may reflect hyperparameter mismatch rather than fundamental limitations.

Time budgets are inconsistent: baselines are run to termination with a 1,000-second cap, while RL-SPH 'stops when all baselines complete their search' (Section 4.1.2), so PG and PI are not necessarily compared at equal wall-clock times. In addition, PG and FT are averaged only over instances where a feasible solution was found, which can flatter methods with low FR.

The RHF baseline is an aggregate of six rounding heuristics; the paper does not specify whether reported numbers are best-of-family, average, or selected per instance, making the '28.6x lower primal gap' claim difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The best-performing RL-SPH variant uses LP relaxation solved by an external LP solver, contradicting the strong framing of 'independently' generating feasible solutions without external solvers. The random-initialized variant avoids LP but is substantially worse on NBI and slower than RHF on IS/MVC (Table 1).

Action space is limited to ±1 per variable per step, and phase2 rolls back all non-improving moves, so the method cannot efficiently handle large integer ranges or escape plateaus. The paper acknowledges this as future work, but it limits current scalability and quality.

MIPLIB results are mixed and appear selectively reported: RL-SPH is much worse than RHF on several instances (scpk4 13,672 vs 765; bppc8-02 1,824 vs 530; toll-like 1,774 vs 1,314), and only 17 MIPLIB instances are shown with no success rate over a larger set (Table 12).

No code or dataset release is provided, and several implementation details (e.g., the exact training phase transition in Algorithm 3 and reward scaling) are hard to reproduce, weakening reproducibility.

Presentation issues: the reward equations (Eqs. 2-8) are dense and ambiguous, notation is inconsistent, and the training procedure in Algorithm 3 is confusing (e.g., resetting to S0 when a feasible solution is found before T_stay).

Some claims are overstated: 'first E2EPH to establish theoretical reward-feasibility alignment' and 'outperforming seven baselines' are not supported; the 28.6x/2.6x averages rely on selective comparisons and exclude cases where a baseline is stronger.

strengths: Addresses a practically important bottleneck in ML for ILP: independently generating feasible solutions, especially for non-binary integer variables, without relying on an external solver to repair infeasibility.

Proposes a coherent RL-based start primal heuristic with a two-phase reward design, feasibility-aware variable selection, and an ILP-tailored graph transformer; ablations support the value of the variable selection and transformer components.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five ILP benchmarks, E2EPH/SPH baselines, cross-problem generalization, MIPLIB instances, solver integration, distribution/size/density shifts, and hyperparameter/qualitative analyses.

Reports 100% feasibility rate on the evaluated benchmarks and strong primal gap/primal integral/first-feasible-time results, with some negative results (e.g., MIPLIB scpk4, bppc8-02) discussed honestly.

Training efficiency is favorable relative to several E2EPH baselines, and the method does not require near-optimal labels; implementation details and hyperparameters are largely provided, supporting reproducibility.
Limitations and promising extensions (scalability, movement magnitude, nonlinear constraints, optimality improvements) are discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is overstated: Proposition 1 is conditional and nearly definitional. It assumes R_{t,const}>0 and R_{t,bound}=0 for all relevant steps, which already implies constraint violations are monotonically decreasing, and it does not prove that reward maximization under the RL dynamics will actually satisfy these conditions.

The claim of 'theoretical reward-feasibility alignment' is therefore weak; the empirical adherence rate of 95.2% is not a theoretical guarantee, and the 4.8% of trajectories that deviate are acknowledged but not analyzed theoretically.

The main SPH comparison disables presolving and branching and lets RL-SPH terminate when all baselines finish; this may not be a fully neutral comparison, even if intended to isolate heuristic performance. Standard solver settings could change relative results.

E2EPH comparisons on SC and CA involve datasets and configurations that differ from those used by the original DiffILO/PAS methods; some failures may be due to distribution shift or tuning sensitivity rather than only feasibility limitations, despite the paper's discussion of this issue.

The reward and search design contain many hand-tuned constants (e.g., R_F scaling, -100 exploration penalty, bound-penalty scaling, alpha, seed/neighbor ratios). Some are ablated, but not all, making robustness and transfer to new ILP families less certain.

Scalability remains a concern: variable selection is O(mn), and the Transformer attention is quadratic in the selected sequence length. The paper tests up to larger instances and MIPLIB, but quality can degrade substantially on very large, dense, or special-constraint instances.

Reproducibility is mostly good but not perfect: random seeds for RL training are not fully specified, and there is no explicit link to the authors' RL-SPH code, though external component code is referenced.
Presentation has some notation inconsistencies (e.g., \hat{n} vs \tilde{n}) and the main paper relies heavily on appendices for core justification and analyses.
